newsitem.title: USA: Boston protests against proposed football stadium.
newsitem.headline: Boston protests against proposed football stadium.

text.p: The city of Boston is like no other in America -- it bans things. In the old days, it banned risque books, shows and records. Now it wants to ban a football stadium.

Specifically it wants to ban a new stadium in south Boston for the New England Patriots, who on Sunday could become the most important football team in the world if they beat the Green Bay Packers in the Super Bowl.

The issue has become a political football. The mayor of Boston, Thomas Menino, does not want it built in south Boston because the 45,000 largely Irish-American blue-collar residents there do not want the noise and traffic jams that are sure to follow.

The governor of Massachusetts, William Weld, however, wants it in South Boston. The state agency, Massport, which controls the land for the proposed site, said Thursday it would move ahead with studies for a stadium there while at the same time exploring other options.

The Massport meeting lasted five hours and produced fireworks and angry charges from south Boston political representatives. One state senator said he was going ahead with a lawsuit to block the stadium.
When Menino and Weld appeared before 20,000 to 30,000 football fans at a Patriots rally in Boston on Sunday, people shouted "stadium" and booed the mayor when he spoke.

The mayor, fighting a painful kidney stone, signed a letter from his hospital bed Wednesday blasting Massport. "Long after the the football season has ended, the people of Boston and the neighborhood of South Boston will live with the consequences of your decision," Menino wrote.

Weld, meanwhile, is riding the public frenzy over the Patriots, but an adviser admitted if the Patriots lost the Super Bowl, or Coach Bill Parcells quit the team as is widely expected, it could derail the governor's momentum.
"A lot of air goes out of the balloon," if the Patriots lose, the source told the Boston Herald.

Congressman Joseph Moakley, who represents South Boston, stepped into the fray Thursday and urged Massport not to authorize the lease. Moakley said he would try to block Patriots owner Bob Kraft from leasing five acres of U.S. Army-owned land adjoining the stadium site where a parking lot is proposed.
The Patriots' current stadium is 40 miles south of Boston in Foxboro, Massachusetts, just a short drive away from Providence, Rhode Island, a city that would like to claim the Patriots as their own.

The team's current stadium is a crumbling, concrete, open-air facility that even the National Football League considers one of the worst. "It's the Roman Coliseum ... antiquated and decrepit," NFL spokesman Greg Aiello said.
Power failed there during a game two weeks ago and the plumbing does not work well either. Parcells has complained of pipes bursting in his office.
Just about everyone, including the team's owner Robert Kraft, agrees that Foxboro is in bad shape and the team needs a new stadium. The question is where?
Rhode Island Gov. Lincoln Almond and Providence Mayor Vincent "Buddy" Cianci have moved swiftly to offer potential sites for a new Patriot stadium.

But team owner Kraft wants South Boston and the chance to put in skyboxes that would bring millions of dollars in revenues despite the protests of the Southies, as residents of south Boston are called.

"I don't see why it should be pushed down their throats and I don't see why the taxpayer should pay it," said Boston Herald columnist and radio personality Howie Carr. "Let's have the Legislature work on making me my first million dollars rather than Bob Kraft's first billion dollars."

Carr said the people of South Boston would rather see "the governor give tax credits for their satellite dishes so they can see the Pats play someplace else than give this guy Kraft all this public money."
